answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
Consequential accounting can materially improve decision‑usefulness by estimating the system‑wide emissions impact of discrete electricity actions relative to a counterfactual baseline, rather than allocating existing emissions within organisational boundaries. It is especially valuable in electricity because marginal impacts depend on which generators are “on the margin”, which vary by time, grid region, and operating conditions.
Benefits: (1) Enables better prioritisation of actions that genuinely reduce system emissions (e.g., shifting load away from high marginal‑emissions hours; deploying firm low‑carbon supply where marginal generators are fossil). (2) Improves integrity of impact claims by distinguishing attributional inventory outcomes from consequential avoided‑emissions outcomes. (3) Supports grid‑relevant investment signals by reflecting operational and longer‑term structural impacts.

Challenges: (1) Data and modelling intensity: high‑quality marginal emissions estimation requires transparent dispatch/price/constraint information or credible published datasets; many regions lack this. (2) Comparability: differing methods (SCED, statistical, LMP/heat‑rate, scenario, etc.) can yield materially different results if not standardised. (3) Uncertainty and perceived “precision”: sub‑hourly/nodal claims may imply false accuracy where inputs are sparse or confidential. (4) Risk of misinterpretation: consequential metrics should not be conflated with Scope 2 inventory totals; guidance should require clear claim language, boundaries, and uncertainty disclosure.

Unintended consequences: Poorly governed approaches may incentivise “impact shopping” (seeking high marginal‑emissions regions purely to maximise claimed avoided emissions), or undermine confidence if claims are inconsistent across methods. Additionally, actions that reduce transmission losses/congestion (or increase curtailment) may be under‑reflected if frameworks focus narrowly on generation dispatch outcomes without appropriate disclosure of whole of system conditions.

Practical recommendations: (a) Provide tiered method options with minimum data/quality requirements and default conservative options where data are limited. (b) Require transparent disclosure of method, spatial/temporal resolution, uncertainty, and whether OM/BM are included. (c) Maintain strict separation between consequential “impact” metrics and attributional inventories.

answers.label: Appropriateness of the TWG subgroup formula
Why the formula is or is not appropriate
answers.text:
Yes — the formula is structurally appropriate for quantifying emissions impacts, because it links electricity project impacts to marginal emission rates at the time and location of grid interaction, consistent with how consequential impacts occur in real systems.
The formula intentionally focuses on the baseline emissions side of the equation (MWh × marginal emission rate) and leaves project scenario emissions to be calculated separately, as described in the underlying Guidelines for Grid‑Connected Electricity Projects and Project Accounting Protocols.

This separation is important because technology efficiency is captured entirely within the project scenario, not in the baseline formula. For example, solar PV efficiency losses (inverter losses, temperature derating, DC–AC conversion) affect the actual MWh generated, which directly affects avoided emissions. The Protocol notes that renewable project emissions are usually zero, so their efficiency is inherently accounted for in the MWh delivered.

Likewise, for storage technologies such as pumped hydro, which have round‑trip inefficiencies, the consequential method accounts for these via the project scenario emissions calculation: energy consumed during pumping (charged with grid electricity at its own marginal emission rate) minus energy generated during discharge. The guidelines explicitly define project primary‑effect emissions as the project’s own emissions rate multiplied by its generation, and the project scenario always includes any electricity consumed by the project.
Thus, efficiency is implicitly but fully captured through the project scenario, not the baseline formula.

The formula is therefore appropriate, provided that guidance continues to require (1) consistent treatment of project scenario emissions (including efficiency and energy consumption), (2) transparency in marginal emission rate datasets, and (3) clear disclosure of whether OM‑only or OM+BM impacts are included.

answers.label: Secondary effects to consider, and how
answers.text:
Secondary effects should be considered where they are material and reasonably quantifiable, consistent with existing project accounting principles. The consultation notes that secondary effects may include one time construction/decommissioning emissions and upstream/downstream impacts (e.g., fuel supply chain changes), and also notes that it is not necessary to conduct a full lifecycle analysis—only significant effects should be included.

Recommended approach:
- Apply a materiality threshold (e.g., include secondary effects when expected to exceed a few percent of the primary effect), and require justification for exclusions.
- Prioritise secondary effects most relevant to electricity projects, such as:
o construction and decommissioning emissions where OM dominates (or where project/baseline differ materially
o upstream fuel supply chain impacts where projects materially change fuel extraction/transport patterns, and
o significant land use or reservoir methane effects for certain technologies (where applicable).
o Use conservative defaults where data are limited, with transparent disclosure.

This balances integrity with feasibility and avoids overburdening reporters for immaterial effects.

answers.label: Why annual or lifetime reporting
answers.text:
Report annually to align with reporting cycles and changing grid conditions. The consultation notes that marginal generators and marginal emission rates vary by hour, season, and system evolution; annual reporting keeps consequential results current and decision-useful.

Annual reporting also better reflects changes in project performance over time (e.g., PV degradation, operational changes, and storage round-trip efficiency and dispatch behaviour), which affect delivered MWh and electricity consumed and, therefore, change the project’s consequential impact. Lifetime “once-off” estimates can be useful for investment appraisal, but they rely on long-range assumptions about future dispatch, policy, and grid build/retirements, which can reduce comparability and transparency. Project accounting guidance recognises baseline validity and the choice of static vs dynamic assumptions; annual reporting is a practical way to update and disclose evolving assumptions.

Recommendation: require annual reporting for public claims, while allowing an optional supplemental lifetime estimate for internal appraisal with clear uncertainty disclosure.

answers.label: Requiredness of the financial analysis test
Requiredness of the common practice test
Why selected tests should be included
answers.text:
A robust additionality framework should minimise non-additional crediting while remaining feasible across regions. Project accounting guidance recognises additionality as critical for integrity and highlights the need to balance stringency vs participation; no single test is sufficient alone.

- Regulatory (Required): prevents claims for actions mandated by law/policy—foundational for integrity.
- Timing (Required): reduces “already underway” claims by showing the incentive/claim mechanism influenced the investment decision. Common practice (Required): avoids crediting activities that are already mainstream without incentives and supports comparability.
- Financial analysis (Optional): strong evidence where feasible, but can be confidential/burdensome, best as an optional pathway with documentation.
- Barrier (Optional): useful where qualitative constraints dominate, but can be subjective, should require clear evidence and a transparent narrative.
- Performance standards and positive lists (Optional): can reduce transaction cost and improve scalability but require strong governance, periodic updates, and stringency to avoid crediting non-additional actions.
- Contractual/tenor and first-of-its-kind (Optional): useful supporting indicators (e.g., long-term PPAs for financing certainty; early deployments facing higher risk) but not definitive alone; should sunset once replicated/common.

answers.label: Context on test feasibility
answers.text:
- Regulatory and timing tests are generally feasible because they rely on observable policy settings and documented project timelines/commitments.
- Common practice is feasible where credible market penetration data exists; where it does not, guidance should allow conservative proxies or regional defaults with disclosure.
- Financial and barrier tests can be powerful but are often less feasible due to confidentiality, data access, and subjective judgments about causality; therefore, they are best offered as optional pathways with clear documentation requirements.
- Performance standards and positive lists are feasible only if centrally governed, stringent, and regularly updated to remain representative.

answers.label: Additionality tests missing from the framework
answers.text:
Additional tests to consider:
1) Investment causality evidence test: requiring credible evidence that the purchaser’s action affected financing/commitment (e.g., lender/board documentation contingent on the contract), as an alternative to full financial model disclosure.

2) Grid/system value test (for impact claims): require disclosure of how the project contributes to system needs (e.g., reliability contribution, curtailment reduction, congestion relief) to reduce “impact shopping” and improve interpretability of avoided-emissions claims.

3) Minimum counterfactual documentation standard: require explicit baseline scenario narrative with minimum supporting documentation, consistent with Project Protocol emphasis on baseline credibility and transparency

4) Demand Reduction / Efficiency Additionality Test: For energy efficiency (EE) and demand‑side interventions, require a credible documented baseline consumption scenario and evidence that the intervention changes that baseline, consistent with GHG Protocol project accounting requirements for establishing credible counterfactual baselines. Electricity‑reduction project activities must quantify avoided generation by converting site-level savings into avoided grid generation, accounting for grid losses (L), as required in the Grid‑Connected Electricity Projects Guidelines. This ensures EE actions are not credited where they reflect business‑as‑usual or endogenous trends.

5) Loss, Congestion & Curtailment Impact Test (Network System-Impact Test): Where a project materially reduces transmission/distribution losses, congestion, or curtailment, or defers network augmentation (e.g., through distributed generation, storage, flexible demand, local solar‑plus‑storage, or feeder‑level upgrades), require disclosure and quantification of these avoided impacts. The Guidelines explicitly state that avoided grid generation must include losses and that these parameters may be monitored and updated over time. Because congestion and curtailment strongly affect which generators are “on the margin,” and affect future grid investment needs, such interventions can have meaningful consequential impacts beyond simple operational displacement, improving both OM and BM accuracy.

6) Structural Persistence / Planning Incorporation Test (Build-Margin Relevance): For interventions claimed to influence the build margin, require evidence that the intervention is persistent and sufficiently material to affect capacity-expansion, retirement, or network‑investment decisions. This may include demonstrated alignment with formal planning processes, scenario modelling, or evidence of peak‑coincident firming/load‑reducing value. The consultation stresses that persistent changes influence long-term structural evolution (BM), whereas short‑term changes affect the operating margin. A persistence/planning relevance test ensures BM impacts are not overstated.

7) Measurement & Verification (M&V) Evidence Test for Efficiency & DER: Require M&V consistent with recognised practice to verify claimed energy savings or demand response impacts. The Guidelines specify that avoided generation must be inferred from measured electricity reductions, and this requires appropriate monitoring and documentation.

Collectively, these additional tests would ensure that efficiency, DER, and loss‑reducing interventions, often undervalued under attributional frameworks, are rigorously assessed for both operating‑margin impact and long‑term structural (build‑margin) relevance.

answers.label: Regions warranting different tests, with examples
answers.text:
Yes—regional differences should be considered because policy contexts, grid mixes, data availability, and market structures vary widely. The consultation notes emissions impacts differ materially by region, depending on marginal generators and the existing supply mix.

Examples: data-rich markets can support rigorous common-practice and performance-standard tests; data-poor markets may need conservative defaults and simplified pathways. Regions with strong renewable mandates/high penetration may require greater reliance on common-practice/regulatory tests, while emerging markets may require barrier/financing evidence pathways. Guidance should allow equivalent-rigour pathways (not one-size-fits-all) with transparent disclosure of the pathway used.

answers.label: Claims possible under different test approaches
answers.text:
Yes—rigour should scale with the strength of the claim. Association/contribution claims (e.g., “supported renewable generation”) may be permitted under simpler evidence pathways. Causal/avoided-emissions claims (“caused X tCO2e avoided”) should require stronger additionality evidence (e.g., regulatory + timing + common practice, plus one of financial/barrier/contractual evidence), consistent with project accounting emphasis on credible baselines and additionality for integrity.

Guidance should also require claim language to specify OM-only vs OM+BM/combined impacts and disclose key assumptions and uncertainty to avoid over-interpretation.

answers.label: Details on operating margin methodologies
answers.text:
OMER methods should prioritise approaches that best approximate marginal redispatch under real grid conditions. SCED-based approaches (fuel-on-margin and locational) and scenario modelling are conceptually strongest where grid-operator data or credible simulations exist, because they reflect dispatch, constraints, and security conditions.

Heat-rate/LMP methods can be appropriate where prices are robust and fuel-cost/technology assumptions are transparent, but require guardrails where prices reflect scarcity, uplift, or non-fuel constraints. Statistical approaches can be appropriate where designed to estimate causal response conditioned on demand/weather/time, but need transparent methods, validation/back-testing, and periodic recalibration.

Capacity-factor and difference-based approaches are useful as screening or fallback in data-poor contexts, but should not be primary methods for project-level impact claims because they can misidentify marginal units and confound outages/constraints and other drivers. If used, require conservative assumptions and clear disclosure of limitations.

answers.label: Details on build margin methodologies
answers.text:
BMER methods should reflect structural grid evolution: what generation is built/retired in response to persistent changes. Capacity expansion modelling and policy scenarios are conceptually strong where assumptions, boundaries, and update cadence are transparent, because they explicitly simulate build/retirements under constraints.

Recent capacity additions can be appropriate where build trends are stable and datasets are credible, but must be assessed for representativeness in rapidly transitioning systems. Average grid emission rates generally do not represent marginal additions/retirements and are not appropriate as a primary BMER proxy; they may be used only as a conservative fallback with disclosure when no credible BMER approach exists.

answers.label: Assessing model applicability to project types
answers.text:
GHG Protocol could assess model applicability using a tiered suitability framework based on system conditions and project characteristics. The consultation emphasises that marginal generators vary by hour, region, and operating constraints, and that both operational and structural impacts must be considered.

Key applicability factors include:
• Project persistence and scale: Persistent or large interventions affect long-term structural evolution (BM relevance), while short-term or non-persistent actions primarily affect OM.

• Shape and peak coincidence: The project’s alignment with peak hours determines whether BM effects are likely (via capacity value) or whether OM-only methods suffice.

• Capacity value / reliability contribution: Projects with firm or peak-coincident output are more likely to influence retirements/new builds and thus require BM-capable models.

• Losses, congestion, and curtailment conditions:
o Where T&D losses are material, OM/BM models must account for avoided generation beyond site-level MWh. The Grid-Connected Electricity Projects Guidelines instruct conversion of electricity savings into avoided grid generation including losses.
o In regions with significant congestion or curtailment, marginal generators may differ across nodes/zones, and MERs may diverge materially. Locational or SCED-based methods become more appropriate. Congestion also affects BM relevance by changing where new capacity is needed.
o Projects that reduce congestion or curtailment (e.g., storage, flexible demand, distributed resources) may require models able to reflect these structural effects, not only operational dispatch.

• Data transparency and operator disclosures: Regions with robust dispatch, pricing, and constraint data can support high-resolution SCED, LMP/heat-rate, scenario, or statistical models; data-poor regions may require conservative fallback methods.

• Technology-specific profiles: Intermittent, firm, storage, or efficiency projects require models capable of capturing their operational dynamics and interactions with congestion and curtailment.

• A tiered applicability approach, selecting methods capable of capturing system characteristics such as losses, congestion, and curtailment, improves accuracy and alignment with consequential accounting principles while maintaining feasibility across diverse regions.

answers.label: Other appropriate emission rates or metrics
answers.text:
Additional metrics can improve interpretability of consequential results, especially in systems where losses, congestion, or curtailment significantly influence which generators are on the margin and how the grid evolves structurally. The consultation highlights that marginal generators vary by time and region, and that consequential assessments depend on system conditions.

Recommended supplementary metrics include:

•Loss-adjusted avoided generation factors: For efficiency, demand response, and distributed energy resources (DER), avoided emissions should reflect avoided grid generation, including T&D losses. The Grid-Connected Electricity Projects Guidelines explicitly require the use of loss factors when converting site-level savings to avoided generation.

• Congestion-adjusted marginal emissions: Congestion alters marginal generator identity and can increase or decrease the emissions intensity of marginal dispatch. Congestion-adjusted MERs help distinguish whether a project relieves or exacerbates constraint-driven redispatch. This supports more accurate OM and BM assessments in constrained systems.

• Curtailment and “renewable displacement risk” indicators: High curtailment zones may cause renewable projects to displace other renewables rather than fossil generation, reducing their consequential avoided emissions. Curtailment-adjusted metrics improve transparency on whether avoided emissions come from fossil displacement or RES displacement.

• Reliability/capacity value metrics (e.g., ELCC): Capacity value informs whether a project contributes to structural adequacy and long-term planning (BM relevance), consistent with the consultation’s distinction between OM and BM.

• Network-augmentation/deferral indicators: Projects that defer upgrades or reduce peak loading on the network (e.g., DER, Feeder-level storage) contribute structural value not captured by MERs alone. Network deferral metrics help contextualise these longer-term build-margin effects.

These metrics complement MER-based calculations by capturing factors ( losses, congestion, curtailment, system peak needs, and network deferral) that meaningfully influence both operating and build-margin emissions impacts.

answers.label: Why that spatial granularity ceiling
answers.text:
Zonal is a practical maximum requirement for global guidance because it captures major locational variation (including congestion effects) without requiring confidential node-level operational data. The consultation notes nodal/sub-hourly datasets exist in some markets, but many jurisdictions do not publish such data; mandating nodal would reduce feasibility and equity.

Recommendation: require zonal/grid-region where that is the highest-credible published boundary; allow nodal where grid operators publish robust nodal marginal emissions (or equivalent) with documented QA/QC, governance, and update cadence, plus clear disclosure.

answers.label: Why that temporal granularity ceiling
answers.text:
Hourly is an appropriate maximum requirement for general guidance because it captures meaningful variation in marginal units across the day and seasons while remaining feasible across many systems. The consultation notes marginal generators change throughout the day and year, and that sub-hourly datasets exist in some markets; however, sub-hourly should be optional due to availability, comparability and assurance constraints.

Recommendation: require hourly where available; allow coarser temporal proxies only where no higher-resolution data exist, with conservative assumptions and transparent disclosure of limitations and uncertainty.

answers.label: Appropriate margin weighting approaches
selections: GHG Protocol Guidelines for Quantifying GHG Reductions from Grid-connected Electricity Projects

answers.label: Why selected weighting approaches are appropriate
answers.text:
The GHG Protocol grid-connected electricity guidelines are appropriate because they provide a structured logic for determining whether BM, OM, or both apply, including consideration of capacity demand/under-capacity and capacity value/firmness, and provide defaults where precise inputs are unavailable.

Resource adequacy approaches are appropriate because they use established power-system metrics (capacity value/contribution to peak reliability) that map directly to how persistent interventions influence long-term capacity planning and retirements (build margin impacts). Intervention lifecycle approaches are promising for feasibility because they recognise that OM impacts can dominate initially but BM effects emerge as the system adapts over time; lifecycle rules can improve consistency and reduce discretion.

UNFCCC CDM Tool07 can be useful as a pragmatic approach in some contexts, but fixed weights by technology can misrepresent system conditions and should be applied cautiously with disclosure. A universal 0.50 BM default is simple but can be materially wrong for many interventions and should not be the primary method.

answers.label: Weighting approaches not feasible to implement
Why selected weighting approaches are infeasible
answers.text:
Feasibility depends on regional data and institutional context. Resource adequacy approaches can be difficult where capacity value metrics are not published or planning processes are opaque. Intervention lifecycle approaches require credible evidence of whether and when an intervention is reflected in planning (or robust proxies), which may not exist in all markets.

To improve feasibility and equity, GHG Protocol could provide tiered options:
(1) a guideline-based default method,
(2) higher-rigour methods where data exist (resource adequacy/locational), and
(3) conservative fallbacks with required disclosures where proxies are used.

answers.label: Other approaches for assigning margin weights
answers.text:
A practical alternative is a tiered combined-margin approach:

• Tier 1 (data-rich): OM from published marginal emissions (SCED/statistical/LMP) and BM from capacity expansion/policy scenarios; weight using capacity value/resource adequacy metrics.

• Tier 2 (moderate data): OM from zonal/hourly marginal factors; BM from recent capacity additions; weight using guideline defaults based on firmness and peak coincidence.

• Tier 3 (data-poor): OM and BM using conservative proxy factors and conservative weights, with explicit uncertainty disclosure.
This aligns with the consultation’s distinction between OM and BM and with project accounting principles supporting transparency, consistency, and conservative assumptions where uncertainty is high.

answers.label: Research supporting the suggested approach
answers.text:
Support is provided by existing GHG Protocol guidance and the consultation framing:

• The Grid-Connected Electricity Projects guidelines describe how projects affect BM and OM and provide a structured method for assigning weights based on capacity demand, firmness/capacity value, with defaults where precise inputs are unavailable.

• The consultation distinguishes operating-margin (short-term marginal dispatch) from build-margin (long-term structural) impacts and highlights the need to combine/weight these effects for persistent interventions.

• The Project Protocol sets principles for baseline credibility, transparency, consistency, and conservative assumptions under uncertainty, supporting tiered methods and defensible fallbacks.
